paragraphs.heading: A wave far above the rest
paragraphs.text: A rogue wave is an open-water wave far bigger than the waves around it. It goes by other names too, such as freak, monster or killer wave, and near the shore it is sometimes called a sneaker wave. Oceanographers draw the line precisely: a rogue wave stands more than twice as tall as the significant wave height, which is the average of the largest third of the waves in a record. These waves are hard to predict and can be deadly to ships and to lone structures such as lighthouses.

paragraphs.heading: How they form
paragraphs.text: No single cause explains them. Sometimes currents or strong winds make waves move at different speeds, so several of them merge into one huge wave. In other cases, nonlinear effects move energy between waves until one becomes extremely large. Studies of a wave pattern called the Peregrine soliton point to a process named modulational instability, in which an ordinary wave starts drawing energy from nearby waves and briefly grows very large.

paragraphs.heading: Not a tsunami
paragraphs.text: Rogue waves are not tsunamis. A tsunami comes from a huge displacement of water, often when the ocean floor moves suddenly, and it is barely noticeable in deep water, turning dangerous only near the shore; in the 2004 Asian tsunami, every ship lost was in port. A rogue wave has nothing to do with land movement: it is brief, local and most often found far out at sea. It also differs from a hundred-year wave, which is just a statistical label for a very high wave with a 1% chance of happening in a given year in a particular body of water.

paragraphs.heading: From legend to measurement
paragraphs.text: For a long time rogue waves were treated as myths, backed only by sailors' accounts and damaged ships. The first scientific evidence came in 1984, when the Gorm platform in the central North Sea recorded an 11 m wave in a relatively low sea. The case that caught scientists' attention was the Draupner wave, measured digitally at a North Sea platform on 1 January 1995, with a maximum height of 25.6 m. It caused minor damage to the platform high above the water, confirming the reading from a laser sensor pointed down at the sea.

paragraphs.heading: Why the old models missed them
paragraphs.text: Disbelief ran deep. In 1826 the French naval officer Jules Dumont d'Urville reported waves of up to 33 m in the Indian Ocean and was publicly ridiculed, at a time when most people held that no wave could top 9 m. From the 19th century on, engineers and ship designers predicted wave heights with a Gaussian model, which assumes heights cluster tightly around the significant wave height. In a storm with a significant wave height of 12 m, that model says a wave over 15 m would hardly ever happen, and a 30 m wave only once in 10,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: Records and losses
paragraphs.text: Later measurements showed how big these waves can get. In February 2000 the British research ship RRS Discovery, in the Rockall Trough west of Scotland, met individual waves up to 29.1 m. In 2004, scientists combing three weeks of satellite radar images from the European Space Agency found ten rogue waves of 25 m or more. Ordinary ocean-going ships are not designed for such encounters, and rogue waves are now proven to have sunk some, such as the freighter MS München in 1978. In 2007 NOAA compiled a catalog of more than 50 past incidents probably linked to them.
